slice: Normalize floating USING and NATURAL join keys
status: optional planner follow-up; default vendor unchanged

protocol.scope: Use the existing Spark predicate coercion for numeric floating USING and NATURAL join keys; preserve merged and qualified output columns and existing ordinary column-key joins.
coverage: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, LEFT SEMI, LEFT ANTI
signed zero, duplicate keys, NULL, NaN, infinities
merged-key sign and schema type; qualified hidden keys
integer/Decimal controls, empty natural keys and name errors
limits: General Spark common-type behavior of a FULL JOIN merged key with mixed integer/Decimal and FLOAT is separate; precision cases project IDs only.
No GROUP BY or DISTINCT fix in this slice.

implementation.rule: Resolve USING/NATURAL key pairs through the existing Spark equality helper, then supply its normalized operands to native DataFusion join_with_expr_keys. Use both input schemas for semi/anti joins. Preserve the original column-key builder when keys are unchanged.
implementation.reuse: Existing Spark normalization/coercion and native HashJoinExec; no new execution kernel, dependency or Python runtime path.
implementation.output: Keep original input columns for merged-key output. Qualified hidden-key lookup still has a pre-existing alias-resolution error.

provenance.implementation: Reuse local spark_binary_expr and DataFusion 54.1.0 join_with_expr_keys; keep original column-key construction when the helper leaves keys unchanged.

correctness.error_text_note: Seven existing failed casts report a different invalid input value; no status, rows, types or other actual fields change.
correctness.join_plan_check: All twelve new benchmark cases use HashJoinExec. Only four existing formatted USING plans change; outputs and other check fields match.

performance_protocol.purpose: Measure USING key normalization and compare it with the existing explicit ON path on the same runtime. Integer USING and ON controls preserve ordinary column keys.
performance_protocol.inference: Use process medians, paired quartet log ratios and fixed seed 172 / 10000 bootstrap resamples. Retain all controls and observations.
performance_protocol.runtime: 35e51d6 optional runtime plus only USING/NATURAL key integration; no type-inference shortcut
performance_protocol.input_limit: Float timings use positive finite keys and equal outputs; signed zero, NULL and nonfinite join semantics are checked in the Spark corpus.

performance_findings: Floating USING execution costs about 2-5 percent more with 2.8-5.2 percent more instructions. Normalization adds about 17 percent planning work. This local cost remains.
Explicit ON and integer join execution instruction counts are unchanged within 0.01 percent. Integer USING planning instructions rise 0.34 percent from shared key inspection.
Candidate FLOAT/DOUBLE USING execution medians are 6.642/6.892 ms, close descriptively to existing explicit ON at 6.645/6.896 ms. This is not a separately paired equivalence test.
All 384 measured processes and same-binary controls are retained. Timing variation is not evidence of zero global overhead.
source_difference: The benchmark builds differ only in resolver/query/join.rs; benchmark, dependency and other runtime sources are identical. Both full correctness captures are fresh.
limitations: Eight qualified hidden-key observations and two duplicate-key observations still differ. No field-resolution policy is changed in this slice.
Four old signed-zero GROUP BY observations remain. General DISTINCT/set operations and mixed FLOAT/integer/Decimal FULL JOIN merged-key common types are not covered.
The coarse corpus excludes schema metadata and structured error equality and is not complete Spark compatibility.
Measurements are bounded to this machine, preloaded inputs and the fixed schedule. Dynamic FLOAT/INT predicate widening remains a separate cost.
The separate type-inference shortcut stays deferred and unapplied. No original timing interval is declared resolved.
